USS Illini
University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
Section: Uncrewed Craft
Matthew Bianchi, Noah Brody, Carter Eid, Sebastian Sanchez, Allan
Zhu, Ethan Cho, Xiaorui Gu, Hongbo Nie, Kevin Ho, Drew Stadelman
 Contents

The University of Illinois has dedicated ten undergraduate seniors in mechanical engineering to
complete the unmanned watercraft that was started in the Spring of 2024, such that it may race in
April of 2025. Through the two previous semesters, some responsibilities of building a competitor
from scratch have been relieved, while many remain for us to address.
Our team has been provided with functional motors, batteries, transmitter, receiver, a workshop,
and other miscellaneous components. We have damaged electronic speed controllers and a
unseaworthy boat hull.
Background Research
Many of our breakthroughs in development were products of quality questions asked and extensive
research undertaken. Initially, our most pressing questions related to general fabrication and design
directions.
Hull Selection
We needed to settle upon a hull shape that prioritized stability as to protect our vital electronics
and payload. Thus, our search became a question of which boat hull provided the greatest level of
stability when exposed to external forces. Stability is defined by Sunaryo et al. [1] as the natural
self-righting force of a body that results from a moment pair between the center of gravity of the
boat and its instantaneous center of buoyancy. See Figure 1 below.
Figure 1. Positive and Negative Self-Righting Force
It is clear to see that a stable hull design would have a sharp increase in the righting moment as a
function of the heeling angle of the boat. Essentially, a stable hull design will aggressively attempt
to righten itself even at small rocking angles. To analyze this property, Sunaryo et al. used Maxsurf
software to plot the self-righting moment of the catamaran style boat as a function of heeling angle,
shown in Figure 2. The steep increase in rightening moment at small heeling angles is readily
observed. Figure 2. Self-Righting Moment vs. Heeling Angle

The catamaran is composed of two thin hydrodynamic hulls mounted side by side. The wide base
of the catamaran explains the great level of stability present in Figure 2. The simulation ran by
Sunaryo et al. provided insight to our team to help select a proper hull. Namely, we were to search
for a hull that strongly and quickly wanted to righten itself even when rocked.
Cooling System
For the motors, batteries, and electronics system to not overheat, an efficient cooling system is
required. Sufficient literature was found on paraffin wax, as well as open and closed loop cooling
systems. These are therefore assumed to be the cooling systems most frequently seen on this type
of watercraft.
Based on the section 4.4 of “A review of thermal performance improving methods of lithium-ion
battery: Electrode modification and thermal management system” written by Zhao, Zhang, et al.
[2], paraffin wax is the most researched method for Li-ion battery cooling for a stationary system.
This solution has a low cost, but it does add substantial weight. A disadvantage of this method is
that paraffin wax has low heat conductivity, meaning not much heat is removed from the system
but rather is stored in the paraffin wax itself. This means that heat surges and extended runtimes
can lead to heat buildup in the wax, increased operating temperature and battery damage.
To compensate, we will be combining our paraffin wax cooling with active heat removal in the
form of an open-water heat exchanger system. We used a patent [3] as reference, which we plan
on improving in our implementation. The patent discusses a system in which water is pumped
from the lake through the cooling system and then back out into the lake–without affecting the
propeller. The craft that the patent was designed for is similar in size to ours with similar needs.
However, the patent warns about shallow waters that may have branches, vegetation, rocks, or
reefs. Our sponsor indicated that for competition in Virginia such items would not be
encountered. Nevertheless, the inlet for the open loop will be covered with a fine mesh, allowing
water to flow freely with minimal minor losses while preventing debris and aquatic flora from
entering and damaging our water pumps. Bang, Jerng, et al. conducted a study [4] on whether open loop or closed loop systems were more

effective in heat removal and overall efficiency. They found that both systems provided sufficient
cooling for their application, and the open system performed better for heat-removal performance.
They warned that with open systems flow instability or different water patterns could affect the
efficiency of the system. However, such aspects are not expected to be seen in the water on
competition day.
Water Sealing
To ensure that the sensitive electronics are protected from splashing, proper water sealing of
internal components is necessary. On a small boat, sealing can be broken down into three parts:
waterproofing of the hull; internal waterproofing of the batteries, wires, and electronics; and active
removal of water using a bilge pump.
In the chapter “Sealants” in the Engineered Materials Handbook Desk Edition [5], the ASM
provides an in-depth analysis of different types of sealants. Pure silicones, as used in the previous
iteration, have excellent performance and can strain more than 25% prior to failure. This process
is critical for a boat hull where waves can create impact loading on the hull. Additionally, silicone
sealants typically last over 10 years, operate at a wide range of temperatures up to 400 °F, and
bond to most surfaces without a primer, although they do take several days to fully cure. Another
option would be to use vinyl plastisol, commonly found in threaded pipe connectors. These also
have excellent flexibility and vibrational resistance, making them an equally viable option for a
boat hull.
A potential plan for the water removal system is from patents such as [6]. This patent proposes a
lightweight bilge pump that can be temporarily fastened anywhere in the bilge, the lowest part of
a vessel to collect water through an integrated strainer. Water is pumped through a low-voltage
inline pump and attachable hose, removing the water over the rails rather than holes drilled in the
hull.
The research done during the background stage provided our team with insight to make grounded
decisions when it came to the design of our boat.
Design & Analysis
Hull Selection & Modification
Hull selected factored in price, workability, hydrodynamics, weight capacity, and size. In the end,
a modified Wave 60 Youth Kayak from Lifetime Fitness was selected as the hull for its competitive
pricing, compact size, and streamlined shape. The kayak was constructed from two layers of blowmolded high-density polyethylene (HDPE). HDPE has exceptional strength-to-weight ratio,
durability, and chemical resistance, while retaining good workability. The team removed the
topmost layer to make room for the boat’s components, lowering the center of gravity and making waterproofing easier. Plastic welding was used to patch drainage holes that were in the hull. An

acrylic lid lays on top of the hull and protects the internal components from splashes and large
waves.
Inspired by the previous team, we also plan to mount catamaran-style stabilizers on either side of
the kayak, as shown in Figure 3. This will greatly increase the hull’s stability on the roll axis.
Figure 3: Rightening Moment Provided by Catamaran-Style Hulls
A quick word on the math shown in the above figure: with the buoy just fully submerged, the force
of buoyancy is a product of gravity, volume of the buoy, and the difference in density between the
buoy and water. The rightening moment is this buoyancy force times the horizontal distance to the
boat. Given that our boat does not have a lot of rotational inertia in the perpendicular axis, the
buoys are modeled to stabilize the boat well.
Component Layout
To maintain a center of gravity in the geometrical center of the boat, the components were
approximated as point-masses and the center of gravity was calculated, as shown in Figure 4.Figure 4. Center of Mass Approximation

Selecting the position of masses B and C, representing the batteries and propulsion equipment
respectively, the position of the payload was solved to be 1.74 meters from the back of the boat.
Since the boat is 1.83 meters, it will be placed in the front of the boat to counteract the mass of the
batteries and propulsion in the rear.
Propulsion Selection
The twin-motor propulsion system is powered by two 56-series 56123/550KV motors from SSS
motors. As these motors are capable of spinning at up to 24,420 RPM with the 44.4V batteries
selected by the electrical team, a 4:1 gearbox from Neugart was selected to improve torque and
reduce the motor speed. However, as the gearbox is only rated to spin at 18,000 RPM, the final
shaft speed becomes 4,500 RPM.
The design team opted for a belt-drive propulsion system, selecting timing belts with a 0.2” pitch
and ⅜” width. A 17” belt diameter was chosen to allow for a propeller clearance of 15% of the
propeller diameter. This allows the team to keep the motors within the hull walls for balance and
waterproofing. The research done on hull sealing will ensure that the housing for the belt is
properly attached and sealed against the outer surface of the hull. Figure 5 shows a CAD design
of the complete propulsion system. Figure 5. CAD design of the complete propulsion system

The propulsion team was left with limited choices for a propeller. With a twin-engine setup, both
left- and right-handed propellers were necessary for smooth operation. Such combinations of
propellers proved difficult to obtain through online shopping, as most boat propellers available
were either hobby-size propellers with a diameter of below 10cm, large, expensive propellers of
diameters of over 30cm intended for manned boats, or available in only left-handed or right-handed,
but not both.
As such, the team opted to 3-D print an open-source propeller design, mirroring the CAD file to
reverse the direction of the propeller and adding additional holes to accommodate the 10mm shaft.
Cooling Selection
To effectively keep our electric propulsion boat cool during operation, we decided to integrate a
dual-strategy approach centered around an open-water heat exchanger system and paraffin wax as
a phase-change cooling agent, inspired and validated by extensive literature review.
Starting with the paraffin wax, this method comes into play due to its proven effectiveness in
thermal management for lithium-ion batteries, as described by Zhao, Zhang, et al [2]. The use of
paraffin wax is particularly appealing because of its low cost, substantial latent heat capacity, and
low toxicity. It is ideal for absorbing and distributing heat during peak load times, as the high latent
heat capacity absorbs large amounts of energy without raising the temperature. Unlike the previous
team’s implementation, we increased the submersion of the batteries from one-third to almost the entire battery, increasing the total heat capacity of the wax and providing a greater area for the heat

to transfer from the batteries into the wax.
For active cooling, we employed an open-water heat exchanger system, as outlined in the patent
we found. This system will use lake water, pumped through dual cooling lines, to absorb heat
directly from the motors, ESCs, and batteries. The design of this system considered the patent’s
discussion on environmental considerations, ensuring that our intake and expulsion mechanisms
will adequately handle potential blockages, despite anticipating clean competition waters. This
method was particularly appealing due to the effectiveness of open systems in heat removal, as
confirmed by the study from Bang, Jerng, et al., who noted that open systems, despite their
susceptibility to flow instability, performed superiorly in their test conditions which are akin to
our competition scenario. In addition to the performance advantages of a open-loop cooling system,
we deemed that it is less complex and lighter than a close-loop cooling system.
These combined methods—utilizing the passive cooling properties of paraffin wax and the
dynamic, active cooling from lake water—ensuring that all high-power components within our
boat remain below the critical temperature threshold of 110°C.
Electronic Design
While many components were inherited from previous teams such that our freedom of selection
was limited, we had to understand exactly what we were working with such that we could
supplement our existing materials with compatible components.
Our team has (8) 44.4v 10000mAh LiPo batteries, with a C rating of 30. With at most (4) batteries
wired in parallel per motor, the effective voltage would remain at 44.4v, while the capacity would
jump to 40000mAh. We chose parallel wiring because keeping the voltage constant and increasing
our battery capacity aligned more with our team’s values of prioritizing completion of the race
over speed. The C-rating indicates a peak current to 1200A for 2 minutes from the four-battery
circuit, although each circuit would include at least 15 ohms of resistance through the high-current
connectors our team is using. Thus, the maximum current that could be delivered to the electronic
components would be ~3A, via Ohm’s law.
With these numbers in mind, our team is currently searching for electronic speed controllers that
can handle 12S LiPo configuration, as that is the voltage of our battery. With each LiPo cell
measuring 3.7V, 12 cells wired in series would sum to 44.4v. Ideally, the speed controllers would
be waterproof, but this would be a risk we would have to mitigate otherwise.
Our Flysky transmitter talks with our Flysky receiver on two channels, both supporting pulsewidth modulation via joystick control. The receiver is powered by a small onboard 4.8V battery.
The two channels will serve to control the left and right motor speed. Simplicity was chosen to
avoid programming errors that may arise from the implementation of more intricate software to
host more intuitive controls. Overview of Build, Fabrication & Testing

Component Layout & Hull Flotation
Our team is not yet ready to assemble with the appropriate components from mentioned above. To
test, water buckets were used to simulate the weight of the final systems, and the boat was placed
in a pool to test floatation. Freeboard length is measured, as well as stability by measuring the rate
at which the boat recovered from external forces rocking it. Different forms of waterproofing were
tested on the previous boat hull as they are the exact same model. Different combinations of
silicones and plastic welding were used on different holes to check watertightness. An additional
HDPE panel was used to seal off the back end of the hull where the waterline rose to about an inch
from the top edge.
Electronic Fabrication Process and Testing
The batteries are wired to a bus bar that collects all the batteries’ current, and outputs them through
8 AWG aluminum wires in conduit, suitable for roughly 50A. There are 150A fuses wired in series
with the main cables to prevent overcurrent. The busbar is shown below in Figure 5.
Figure 5. Battery Bus bar with fuses
To test the busbar, several batteries are wired to it, and the output leads are connected to a test
ESC. The ESC is connected to the motor, and controlled using the transmitter to cycle the motor
through the slowest speed setting through the fastest. The motor, ESC, and batteries are monitored
for excess heat accumulation as well as current and voltage using a multimeter. We are in the process of selecting and purchasing functional ESCs that fit the criteria mentioned

above. When we have them, we will test them by replacing the test ESC in the busbar test described
in the above paragraph.
Cooling System Fabrication and Testing
For the passive cooling component, we've selected paraffin wax for its thermal energy storage
capacity. The paraffin wax left over from the previous semester has hardened and requires
significant effort to reuse, so we will use fresh wax to submerge the batteries in a custom-designed
battery box. This box fits within our hull and is built with a durable Delrin base and acrylic sides,
allowing for easy monitoring of the battery and wax condition.
On the active cooling front, we leveraged existing resources and new purchases to assemble our
system. The pumps were inherited from a previous semester, providing a foundation for the
cooling mechanism. However, we needed to purchase additional components to complete the
system, including cooling lines and adapters, to connect and extend the functionality of the existing
pumps. We also developed a dual cooling line system that utilizes lake water as a coolant,
integrating insights from a relevant patent and our specific design needs. A crucial component of
this system is the customized four-pronged intake system, produced using 3D printing technology.
This intake is connected to mesh-lined cooling lines, specifically designed to prevent clogs from
natural debris like seaweed. This setup is tailored to maximize water flow while minimizing the
risk of blockages, ensuring reliable cooling under the demanding conditions of race environments.
Propulsion System Fabrication and Testing
The team decided to use a dual propeller system with left and right propellers that spin in opposite
directions. This system will increase stability and balance in the boat's movement. The team was
not able to find pre-machined left and right propellers of the desired size. The propulsion team
decided that the propellers would be 3D printed. This ensured that the propellers could be made to
exact specifications, within printing tolerances. Both ABS and PETG were used and tested for
these propellers. Informal testing determined ABS to be the most optimal choice for its impact
resistance. Nylon was considered as a third material if the ABS and PETG were found to be of
insufficient strength.
The selected propeller design features a 200mm diameter, 317mm pitch, and an airfoil design to
maximize speed and efficiency. Therefore, not accounting for slippage, the theoretical speed of
the vessel would be:
317mm/revolution * 4,500 revolutions/minute = 1,426,500 mm/minute = 53.18 miles per hour.
The actual speed will likely be significantly slower due to slippage, motor resistance, and
efficiency concerns. This also does not consider the weight of the boat. However, the presence of
two motors is likely to mitigate concerns regarding motor resistance. A custom mount was 3-D printed to incorporate the motor, pulley, and gearbox. ABS was chosen

for its superior heat resistance compared to PLA and PETG.
As mentioned before, the belt system was selected mainly to keep the motors completely dry. The
lower part of the propulsion system includes the belt drive system below the surface of the boat.
PETG was selected for the 3-D printed shell due to its strong layer adhesion and resistance to
leakage.
To waterproof the propulsion system, the propulsion team plans to laser cut custom EPDM rubber
gaskets between submerged components to mitigate leakage. Rubberized washers were also used
to mitigate leakage for individual holes.
However, the areas of most concern are the propeller shafts, which must spin at over 4000 RPM
while still maintaining watertightness. The propulsion team utilized a stuffing box packed with
marine grease to seal the propeller shaft. This technique is used by many remote-controlled boats
and is effective due to the hydrophobic properties of grease.
To assess potential leakage, the propulsion team conducted an experiment using a power drill to
spin the shaft. One end of the stuffing box was mounted in a plastic tub filled with water,
effectively submerging that end. The grease-packed stuffing box underwent over 30 minutes of
constant rotation from the power drill without a single drop of leakage – enough to drain two fully
charged drill batteries.
Risk
Like all engineering tasks, there exists a difference between the optimal situation and the present
situation. Without unlimited time, money, and manpower, there are existing risks that we must be
aware of. We aim to mitigate the damages of risks that we identify early, during the design and
fabrication stage. Also, there will be inevitable uncertainties on race day that we will have to
control to maintain the highest odds of success. It is in our best interest to be well aware of these
concerns. Maintaining consistency, this chapter will be broken up into subsystems for an intuitive
layout.
Hull and Component Layout
The heavy components matter the most when considering the layout. The batteries are completely
enclosed and will be secured with a custom holder to ensure they stay in place. The batteries and
the required payload will be placed as close to the centerline of the boat as possible to ensure
stability.
To create space for all of the internal components, the inner layer of the kayak was cut out.
Although this solved our spacing problem, it significantly weakened the structural integrity of the
hull. To minimize the risk of hull warpage, the hull team reinforced the hull with aluminum extrusions. However, this method introduced another protentional risk. Holes had to be drilled

directly into the underside of the hull, creating numerous other avenues for water intrusion. To
mitigate this issue, bonded rubber washers were used on the exterior in conjunction with an EPDM
gasket on the interior. Near competition day, applying a layer of marine sealant over each holes
further improve watertightness. Testing proved that even with approximately 100 pounds of weight,
this was sufficient to keep water out.
Electronics
Due to the conductive nature of water, electronics are the most delicate components of the boat.
This means both taking precautions for the individual electronics themselves and managing overall
water leakage into the boat.
For the low-voltage related components, this is most applicable to the ESCs that interface between
the high-voltage battery (energy storage) system and the propulsion system. The precaution that
has been taken is by purchasing and installing ESCs that are waterproof. A receiver will be attached
to the ESC to take signals from our RC controller, which means that jumper wires and header pins
will be present. We will be placing these physical circuits in a waterproof container and installing
holes for necessary cables to run in and out, in which the holes will have watertight seals formed
around them.
Risk related to electronic performance can be related to ensuring that the electronics will have the
endurance required to stay running during the entire race. These risks are well manageable as the
ESCs can be endurance tested before the race, and simulations dealing with ESC thresholds and
engagement levels can be implemented during these testing sessions.
Propulsion
Transmission of rotational power from withinthe hull to the outside necessitates large openings on
the hull. We utilized EPDM rubber gaskets between each submerged component to mitigate
leakage. Bonded sealing washers were also used to mitigate leakage for screw holes that penetrate
the hull. Furthermore, a stuffing box for each propeller shaft ensures that no water enters the hull
through the shaft and belt housing. As mentioned before, the stuffing box uses marine grease due
to its hydrophobic properties.
Rust is not a big worry because the boat will ideally not be submerged long enough for this to
become a problem. The entire boat will be flushed and cleaned after testing to reduce component
degradation before and after the competition.
Cooling
Blockages in the open-water heat exchanger system present one critical risk we must mitigate,
stemming from our use of lake water which might carry debris like seaweed that could clog the
intake or cooling lines. To counter this, we developed a filter that employs a large metal mesh held
in a 3D-printed housing. This design is engineered to deflect larger debris and sustain water intake in the event a large piece of debris does get caught on the filter. We will continuously test and

refine this system based on trial runs to ensure optimal functionality and efficiency.
Another manageable risk is inefficient heat transfer due to insufficient submersion in paraffin wax.
Our design utilizes paraffin wax as a passive cooling agent for the batteries, based on its proven
effectiveness in literature. However, not submerging the batteries sufficiently could lead to
suboptimal heat absorption. Learning from both literature and previous team experiences, we will
enhance the submersion from one-fifth to between one-third and one-half, thus ensuring more
effective heat distribution and mitigation of overheating risks.
There are also risks from potential leakage at external cooling system connections. Our mitigation
strategy includes using reinforced, watertight connections that have been tested to withstand
impacts up to our specified safety threshold. By choosing materials and designs that exceed
standard requirements, we aim to ensure durability and prevent leakage.
However, some risks may need ongoing monitoring due to their less predictable nature. Flow
instability in our open water system is one such challenge. Despite the effectiveness of open
systems in removing heat, unpredictable water conditions will influence their performance. Our
response involves optimizing the intake design to reduce sensitivity to flow variations and
conducting extensive tests under different conditions to gauge potential impacts on performance.
Another concern is the extended cooling times associated with paraffin wax during unexpected
peaks in heat generation. While we have optimized the amount of wax and its distribution, the
inherent properties of paraffin wax limit its ability to quickly absorb and dissipate heat. This issue
will be closely monitored during testing phases to determine if additional cooling strategies or
backup measures are necessary.
Appendix
References
[1]S. Sunaryo and F. Yusro, “Hull Design of Solar Powered Recreational Electric Boat for
Indonesian Waters,” E3S Web of Conferences, vol. 67, p. 03010, 2018, doi:
https://doi.org/10.1051/e3sconf/20186703010.
[2] R. Zhao, S. Zhang, J. Liu, and J. Gu, "A review of thermal performance improving methods
of lithium ion battery: Electrode modification and thermal management system," Journal of
Power Sources, vol. 299, pp. 557-577, Sep. 2015.
[3] C. Angelle, B Bridge, “Boat Hull Cooling and Marine-Drive System with Auxiliary Raw
Water Cooling Reservoir,” US Patent 10,947,890 B2, Mar. 16, 2021
[4] J. Bang, D.-W. Jerng, and H. Kim, "Comparisons of performance and operation
characteristics for closed- and open-loop passive containment cooling system design," Nuclear Engineering and Technology, vol. 53, no. 8, pp. 2499-2508, Aug. 2021.

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1738573321000656
[5] ASM International, “Sealants” in Engineered Materials Handbook Desk Edition. ASM
Digital Library. [Online]. Available: https://doiorg.proxy2.library.illinois.edu/10.31399/asm.hb.emde.a0003048
[6] M. H. Irving and J. A. Kenney, “Battery operated small craft bilge pump,” U.S. Patent
11878770 B2, Jan. 23, 2024
[7] E. Johnson and C. Brown, “Boat shaft seal system,” U.S. Patent 11655014 B2, May 23, 2023

A quick word on the math shown in the above figure: with the buoy just fully submerged, the force
of buoyancy is a product of gravity, volume of the buoy, and the difference in density between the
buoy and water. The rightening moment is this buoyancy force times the horizontal distance to the
boat. Given that our boat does not have a lot of rotational inertia in the perpendicular axis, the
buoys are modeled to stabilize the boat well.
Component Layout
To maintain a center of gravity in the geometrical center of the boat, the components were
approximated as point-masses and the center of gravity was calculated, as shown in Figure 4.Figure 4. Center of Mass Approximation
Selecting the position of masses B and C, representing the batteries and propulsion equipment
respectively, the position of the payload was solved to be 1.74 meters from the back of the boat.
Since the boat is 1.83 meters, it will be placed in the front of the boat to counteract the mass of the
batteries and propulsion in the rear.
Propulsion Selection
The twin-motor propulsion system is powered by two 56-series 56123/550KV motors from SSS
motors. As these motors are capable of spinning at up to 24,420 RPM with the 44.4V batteries
selected by the electrical team, a 4:1 gearbox from Neugart was selected to improve torque and
reduce the motor speed. However, as the gearbox is only rated to spin at 18,000 RPM, the final
shaft speed becomes 4,500 RPM.
The design team opted for a belt-drive propulsion system, selecting timing belts with a 0.2” pitch
and ⅜” width. A 17” belt diameter was chosen to allow for a propeller clearance of 15% of the
propeller diameter. This allows the team to keep the motors within the hull walls for balance and
waterproofing. The research done on hull sealing will ensure that the housing for the belt is
properly attached and sealed against the outer surface of the hull. Figure 5 shows a CAD design
of the complete propulsion system. Figure 5. CAD design of the complete propulsion system
The propulsion team was left with limited choices for a propeller. With a twin-engine setup, both
left- and right-handed propellers were necessary for smooth operation. Such combinations of
propellers proved difficult to obtain through online shopping, as most boat propellers available
were either hobby-size propellers with a diameter of below 10cm, large, expensive propellers of
diameters of over 30cm intended for manned boats, or available in only left-handed or right-handed,
but not both.
As such, the team opted to 3-D print an open-source propeller design, mirroring the CAD file to
reverse the direction of the propeller and adding additional holes to accommodate the 10mm shaft.
Cooling Selection
To effectively keep our electric propulsion boat cool during operation, we decided to integrate a
dual-strategy approach centered around an open-water heat exchanger system and paraffin wax as
a phase-change cooling agent, inspired and validated by extensive literature review.
Starting with the paraffin wax, this method comes into play due to its proven effectiveness in
thermal management for lithium-ion batteries, as described by Zhao, Zhang, et al [2]. The use of
paraffin wax is particularly appealing because of its low cost, substantial latent heat capacity, and
low toxicity. It is ideal for absorbing and distributing heat during peak load times, as the high latent
heat capacity absorbs large amounts of energy without raising the temperature. Unlike the previous

team’s implementation, we increased the submersion of the batteries from one-third to almost the entire battery, increasing the total heat capacity of the wax and providing a greater area for the heat
to transfer from the batteries into the wax.
For active cooling, we employed an open-water heat exchanger system, as outlined in the patent
we found. This system will use lake water, pumped through dual cooling lines, to absorb heat
directly from the motors, ESCs, and batteries. The design of this system considered the patent’s
discussion on environmental considerations, ensuring that our intake and expulsion mechanisms
will adequately handle potential blockages, despite anticipating clean competition waters. This
method was particularly appealing due to the effectiveness of open systems in heat removal, as
confirmed by the study from Bang, Jerng, et al., who noted that open systems, despite their
susceptibility to flow instability, performed superiorly in their test conditions which are akin to
our competition scenario. In addition to the performance advantages of a open-loop cooling system,
we deemed that it is less complex and lighter than a close-loop cooling system.
These combined methods—utilizing the passive cooling properties of paraffin wax and the
dynamic, active cooling from lake water—ensuring that all high-power components within our
boat remain below the critical temperature threshold of 110°C.
Electronic Design
While many components were inherited from previous teams such that our freedom of selection
was limited, we had to understand exactly what we were working with such that we could
supplement our existing materials with compatible components.
Our team has (8) 44.4v 10000mAh LiPo batteries, with a C rating of 30. With at most (4) batteries
wired in parallel per motor, the effective voltage would remain at 44.4v, while the capacity would
jump to 40000mAh. We chose parallel wiring because keeping the voltage constant and increasing
our battery capacity aligned more with our team’s values of prioritizing completion of the race
over speed. The C-rating indicates a peak current to 1200A for 2 minutes from the four-battery
circuit, although each circuit would include at least 15 ohms of resistance through the high-current
connectors our team is using. Thus, the maximum current that could be delivered to the electronic
components would be ~3A, via Ohm’s law.
With these numbers in mind, our team is currently searching for electronic speed controllers that
can handle 12S LiPo configuration, as that is the voltage of our battery. With each LiPo cell
measuring 3.7V, 12 cells wired in series would sum to 44.4v. Ideally, the speed controllers would
be waterproof, but this would be a risk we would have to mitigate otherwise.
Our Flysky transmitter talks with our Flysky receiver on two channels, both supporting pulsewidth modulation via joystick control. The receiver is powered by a small onboard 4.8V battery.
The two channels will serve to control the left and right motor speed. Simplicity was chosen to
avoid programming errors that may arise from the implementation of more intricate software to
host more intuitive controls. Overview of Build, Fabrication & Testing
Component Layout & Hull Flotation
Our team is not yet ready to assemble with the appropriate components from mentioned above. To
test, water buckets were used to simulate the weight of the final systems, and the boat was placed
in a pool to test floatation. Freeboard length is measured, as well as stability by measuring the rate
at which the boat recovered from external forces rocking it. Different forms of waterproofing were
tested on the previous boat hull as they are the exact same model. Different combinations of
silicones and plastic welding were used on different holes to check watertightness. An additional
HDPE panel was used to seal off the back end of the hull where the waterline rose to about an inch
from the top edge.
Electronic Fabrication Process and Testing
The batteries are wired to a bus bar that collects all the batteries’ current, and outputs them through
8 AWG aluminum wires in conduit, suitable for roughly 50A. There are 150A fuses wired in series
with the main cables to prevent overcurrent. The busbar is shown below in Figure 5.
Figure 5. Battery Bus bar with fuses
To test the busbar, several batteries are wired to it, and the output leads are connected to a test
ESC. The ESC is connected to the motor, and controlled using the transmitter to cycle the motor
through the slowest speed setting through the fastest. The motor, ESC, and batteries are monitored
for excess heat accumulation as well as current and voltage using a multimeter. We are in the process of selecting and purchasing functional ESCs that fit the criteria mentioned
above. When we have them, we will test them by replacing the test ESC in the busbar test described
in the above paragraph.
Cooling System Fabrication and Testing
For the passive cooling component, we've selected paraffin wax for its thermal energy storage
capacity. The paraffin wax left over from the previous semester has hardened and requires
significant effort to reuse, so we will use fresh wax to submerge the batteries in a custom-designed
battery box. This box fits within our hull and is built with a durable Delrin base and acrylic sides,
allowing for easy monitoring of the battery and wax condition.
On the active cooling front, we leveraged existing resources and new purchases to assemble our
system. The pumps were inherited from a previous semester, providing a foundation for the
cooling mechanism. However, we needed to purchase additional components to complete the
system, including cooling lines and adapters, to connect and extend the functionality of the existing
pumps. We also developed a dual cooling line system that utilizes lake water as a coolant,
integrating insights from a relevant patent and our specific design needs. A crucial component of
this system is the customized four-pronged intake system, produced using 3D printing technology.
This intake is connected to mesh-lined cooling lines, specifically designed to prevent clogs from
natural debris like seaweed. This setup is tailored to maximize water flow while minimizing the
risk of blockages, ensuring reliable cooling under the demanding conditions of race environments.
Propulsion System Fabrication and Testing
The team decided to use a dual propeller system with left and right propellers that spin in opposite
directions. This system will increase stability and balance in the boat's movement. The team was
not able to find pre-machined left and right propellers of the desired size. The propulsion team
decided that the propellers would be 3D printed. This ensured that the propellers could be made to
exact specifications, within printing tolerances. Both ABS and PETG were used and tested for
these propellers. Informal testing determined ABS to be the most optimal choice for its impact
resistance. Nylon was considered as a third material if the ABS and PETG were found to be of
insufficient strength.
The selected propeller design features a 200mm diameter, 317mm pitch, and an airfoil design to
maximize speed and efficiency. Therefore, not accounting for slippage, the theoretical speed of
the vessel would be:
317mm/revolution * 4,500 revolutions/minute = 1,426,500 mm/minute = 53.18 miles per hour.
The actual speed will likely be significantly slower due to slippage, motor resistance, and
efficiency concerns. This also does not consider the weight of the boat. However, the presence of
two motors is likely to mitigate concerns regarding motor resistance. A custom mount was 3-D printed to incorporate the motor, pulley, and gearbox. ABS was chosen
for its superior heat resistance compared to PLA and PETG.
As mentioned before, the belt system was selected mainly to keep the motors completely dry. The
lower part of the propulsion system includes the belt drive system below the surface of the boat.
PETG was selected for the 3-D printed shell due to its strong layer adhesion and resistance to
leakage.
To waterproof the propulsion system, the propulsion team plans to laser cut custom EPDM rubber
gaskets between submerged components to mitigate leakage. Rubberized washers were also used
to mitigate leakage for individual holes.
However, the areas of most concern are the propeller shafts, which must spin at over 4000 RPM
while still maintaining watertightness. The propulsion team utilized a stuffing box packed with
marine grease to seal the propeller shaft. This technique is used by many remote-controlled boats
and is effective due to the hydrophobic properties of grease.
To assess potential leakage, the propulsion team conducted an experiment using a power drill to
spin the shaft. One end of the stuffing box was mounted in a plastic tub filled with water,
effectively submerging that end. The grease-packed stuffing box underwent over 30 minutes of
constant rotation from the power drill without a single drop of leakage – enough to drain two fully
charged drill batteries.
Risk
Like all engineering tasks, there exists a difference between the optimal situation and the present
situation. Without unlimited time, money, and manpower, there are existing risks that we must be
aware of. We aim to mitigate the damages of risks that we identify early, during the design and
fabrication stage. Also, there will be inevitable uncertainties on race day that we will have to
control to maintain the highest odds of success. It is in our best interest to be well aware of these
concerns. Maintaining consistency, this chapter will be broken up into subsystems for an intuitive
layout.
Hull and Component Layout
The heavy components matter the most when considering the layout. The batteries are completely
enclosed and will be secured with a custom holder to ensure they stay in place. The batteries and
the required payload will be placed as close to the centerline of the boat as possible to ensure
stability.
To create space for all of the internal components, the inner layer of the kayak was cut out.
Although this solved our spacing problem, it significantly weakened the structural integrity of the
hull. To minimize the risk of hull warpage, the hull team reinforced the hull with aluminum extrusions. However, this method introduced another protentional risk. Holes had to be drilled
directly into the underside of the hull, creating numerous other avenues for water intrusion. To
mitigate this issue, bonded rubber washers were used on the exterior in conjunction with an EPDM
gasket on the interior. Near competition day, applying a layer of marine sealant over each holes
further improve watertightness. Testing proved that even with approximately 100 pounds of weight,
this was sufficient to keep water out.
Electronics
Due to the conductive nature of water, electronics are the most delicate components of the boat.
This means both taking precautions for the individual electronics themselves and managing overall
water leakage into the boat.
For the low-voltage related components, this is most applicable to the ESCs that interface between
the high-voltage battery (energy storage) system and the propulsion system. The precaution that
has been taken is by purchasing and installing ESCs that are waterproof. A receiver will be attached
to the ESC to take signals from our RC controller, which means that jumper wires and header pins
will be present. We will be placing these physical circuits in a waterproof container and installing
holes for necessary cables to run in and out, in which the holes will have watertight seals formed
around them.
Risk related to electronic performance can be related to ensuring that the electronics will have the
endurance required to stay running during the entire race. These risks are well manageable as the
ESCs can be endurance tested before the race, and simulations dealing with ESC thresholds and
engagement levels can be implemented during these testing sessions.
Propulsion
Transmission of rotational power from withinthe hull to the outside necessitates large openings on
the hull. We utilized EPDM rubber gaskets between each submerged component to mitigate
leakage. Bonded sealing washers were also used to mitigate leakage for screw holes that penetrate
the hull. Furthermore, a stuffing box for each propeller shaft ensures that no water enters the hull
through the shaft and belt housing. As mentioned before, the stuffing box uses marine grease due
to its hydrophobic properties.
Rust is not a big worry because the boat will ideally not be submerged long enough for this to
become a problem. The entire boat will be flushed and cleaned after testing to reduce component
degradation before and after the competition.
Cooling
Blockages in the open-water heat exchanger system present one critical risk we must mitigate,
stemming from our use of lake water which might carry debris like seaweed that could clog the
intake or cooling lines. To counter this, we developed a filter that employs a large metal mesh held
in a 3D-printed housing. This design is engineered to deflect larger debris and sustain water intake in the event a large piece of debris does get caught on the filter. We will continuously test and
refine this system based on trial runs to ensure optimal functionality and efficiency.
Another manageable risk is inefficient heat transfer due to insufficient submersion in paraffin wax.
Our design utilizes paraffin wax as a passive cooling agent for the batteries, based on its proven
effectiveness in literature. However, not submerging the batteries sufficiently could lead to
suboptimal heat absorption. Learning from both literature and previous team experiences, we will
enhance the submersion from one-fifth to between one-third and one-half, thus ensuring more
effective heat distribution and mitigation of overheating risks.
There are also risks from potential leakage at external cooling system connections. Our mitigation
strategy includes using reinforced, watertight connections that have been tested to withstand
impacts up to our specified safety threshold. By choosing materials and designs that exceed
standard requirements, we aim to ensure durability and prevent leakage.
However, some risks may need ongoing monitoring due to their less predictable nature. Flow
instability in our open water system is one such challenge. Despite the effectiveness of open
systems in removing heat, unpredictable water conditions will influence their performance. Our
response involves optimizing the intake design to reduce sensitivity to flow variations and
conducting extensive tests under different conditions to gauge potential impacts on performance.
Another concern is the extended cooling times associated with paraffin wax during unexpected
peaks in heat generation. While we have optimized the amount of wax and its distribution, the
inherent properties of paraffin wax limit its ability to quickly absorb and dissipate heat. This issue
will be closely monitored during testing phases to determine if additional cooling strategies or
backup measures are necessary.
